## Intent
Hypothesis: a simple identity-ordered layout with no intermediates can approach the streaming ceiling through straightforward sequential particle access.

## Cache saturation
The smallest measured point, N=4000, already exceeds the L1d spill at N≈963, so L1-resident behavior is never observed. From N=4000 to N=65000 — straddling the L2 spill at N≈61680 — cost FALLS sharply from 9.538 to 5.943 ns/p at q=0.01, indicating overhead amortization dominates small N rather than cache residency. Past the L2→DRAM transition the curve stays FLAT: 5.95 at N=262000, rising only to 6.203 at N=4000000, with no spill knee. Death rate raises the floor without reshaping the N-curve: at q=0.25 the same fall-then-flat pattern holds (11.524 → 8.48 → 8.529 ns/p), shifted up ~2.5 ns/p throughout.

## Bandwidth
Peak achieved is 11.44 GB/s at N=65000, q=0.01 — 45% of the 25.22 GB/s streaming ceiling. Bandwidth is flat across large N at every death rate: ~11.4 GB/s at q=0.01, ~10.6 GB/s at q=0.05, ~8.0 GB/s at q=0.25. The algo is compute/overhead-bound, not bandwidth-bound: it never approaches the ceiling and shows no transition toward it at any N. Increasing death rate erodes bandwidth linearly — roughly 3 GB/s lost from q=0.01 to q=0.25 — without introducing N-sensitivity, confirming the bottleneck is per-particle scalar work and branchy scatter logic rather than memory throughput.

## Assembly
The compiler did not vectorize — zero vector-suffixed instructions in 245 insns. All floating-point work is scalar: `ldp s5, s6` and `ldp s7, s16` load individual 32-bit components, `fmul`, `fadd`, `fsub` operate on scalar S registers, and `fcvtzs` converts one value at a time. Grid writes are byte-granular: `ldrb`/`strb` pairs read-modify-write individual RGB bytes at computed offsets (`lsl x1, x1, #2`; `add x1, x23, x1`), with `csel` clamping each channel to 0xFF. There is no gather — all loads are direct scalar. The 20 branches, 20 `csel`, and 16 `strb` per particle explain the 45%-of-ceiling cap: the kernel is branch-and-scatter limited, not memory-limited.

## Verdict
Refuted — the algo never exceeds 11.44 GB/s (45% of the 25.22 GB/s ceiling) at any N or death rate, because the compiler emitted entirely scalar code (0 vector instructions) with byte-granular scatter stores (`strb`) that cannot stream. Even in the best case (q=0.01, N=65000, 5.943 ns/p), per-particle cost reflects scalar arithmetic and branchy RGB clamping, not memory bandwidth. The simple identity-ordered layout without intermediates does not approach the streaming ceiling.
